verbatim: The fingerprint machinery and capability ladder and all other machinery are supposed to work in harmony with each other. There is no reason why any of this should no either work, work in the envisaged way, and work in harmony with everything else in the harness as a whole. The singe unifying goal of this project has been that of a science/STEM calculator, problem entered into the system and a definitive, reliable, repeatable answer out, just as is the case with any normal calculator. Does it just stay in that upper league, do we create a new upper league for the more capable models, and how do we tell at any given time which models ae more and which are less capable than others, especially from a cold start at the beginning of an experiment? My initial instinct, without having read anything that has been written so far is in a cold start condition to at first give all the models a very hard randomly generated maths problem to solve, and then only promote the top performing models to the ‘top league’. The top performers would be those who solved the problem the fastest, using tools and writing proofs/falsifiers to validate/disprove the maths problem, and who did so in the most overall cost effective way. This could give you your initial ‘rankings’ I presume? Then for models that performed less well you could assign them a less complex maths problem, and then assess the best performing models in that less demanding position, and you could theoretically continue to do this until the best overall ranking of all available models and the best and most efficient allocation of available resources had been achieved? But surely this is a question that has been asked in computer science before? I cannot be the only person in the history of computer science who has ever wondered what the best and most efficient way to allocated available resources, CPU/GPU, memory and storage capacity and cost (although cost needn’t be a primary factor at this time, as it might be difficult to always reliably calculate, beyond perhaps a reported estimate) unless a researcher ran all models through a single resource like OpenRouter, which of course (like me) a researcher may not always be inclined, or be able to do.) So time for a little, or perhaps a lot of reading I think. How does my (possibly rather crude idea stack up against the competition? Are we attempting to reinvent the wheel? How do other project that us a similarly distributed compute model like Folding@Home, Seti@Home, Einstein@Home and others (although you shouldn’t just restrict your reading to projects of this nature) tackle the same problem? Obviously it doesn’t make sense to pitch a little desktop PC, against an entire vast supercomputer/server stack, so how exactly should we tackle this? That said, ultimately CDSFL was always envisaged from the outset to be capable of running on similar principles to these projects, although ultimately preferably we could go one step further and require no central server at all (except that required by the models participating in an experiment themselves), and that as well as running in standard configuration, as we are doing and have done from the outset of this project, the system should be capable of running in peer to peer mode too (a bit like bit torrent). We had a lot of discussion about this quite early on in the project, but I don’t know if any work was done, or if anything was ever actually built, or if it is even still useful if it was built? So as well as doing external research, rather than have me repeat the whole conversation again, please do some deep archaeology on these specific discussions, to see if there is anything there that might help resolve our problem, or at least where on our design journey these capabilities should be built on our roadmap/runway, if indeed they are not already?

title: Something I have been mulling over all night too is again the cold start issue in any given experiment. Since we can’t k
verbatim: Something I have been mulling over all night too is again the cold start issue in any given experiment. Since we can’t know immediately what resources we have, at the outset of an experiment, or how well the models might perform, or what their rankings should be, the only solution I could potentially come up with was indeed again taken from our football analogy. Here during winners cup draws, or the European league, smaller less capable teams can sometimes be randomly picked to run against much bigger, much more capable teams/players. Sometimes this can indeed be done via a coinflip, but most often its done by randomly selecting names of ‘clubs’ from a silk bag. So at the beginning no capability of any team or player is simply assumed, They are simply randomly selected and through each successful wining round, the winning teams/players then play against each other in a matched pair, then the process repeats itself until only the top ranking players and teams are pitched against each other. I don’t know if this together with my previous observation resolves anything? Butin the real world, this usually ends up with only the best top players and teams matched against each other, where other lesser players/teams sit further down in the league table. The problem is when we push the football analogy too far, and start saying thee should be x number of ‘leagues’, and y number of players, or payers should have special names like football stars that get them more recognition than others, or when we start talking about should thee not just be individual players, but actual whole teams? No none of that needs to be true, surely, because first we are not actually playing football, so there is no requirement for us to follow exactly the rules that football follows, and secondly the football analogy is just that an analogy. We shouldn’t have out code littered with football references,, or talk of ‘defenders’, or strikers, or even ‘leagues’, as such or anything like that. The purpose of using an algology is simply to help us decide how things in a complex environment of exactly the kind we are considering might be best allocated and utilised. Not to turn CDSLF into a literal (if slightly overengineered) version of Fifa Football manager 2027! So in reality there should probably be no distinction between models participating in an experiment other than a ‘ranking number’, or some equivalent, or better methodology that might arise from your own work, or your research. As I said previously, although quite a lot of water has flowed under the bridge since I first said it earlier yesterday, the only things that should denote a model’s ranking in any given experiment is derived/demonstrable capability, either above that. Or below that of is peers. With each direction determining its ranking during an experimental run. So we just need to find a way that resolves these problems comprehensively. That’s all.

title: 300 attempts for a single model to solve any given problem is clearly vastly much too much! For the entire majority of a
verbatim: 300 attempts for a single model to solve any given problem is clearly vastly much too much! For the entire majority of almost every experiment we have ever run, this would almost certainly cause the needle of a models ranking to barely move and to probably never move at all. Ae you even checking if these numbers make any practical sense before writing them? To go back to our football analogy, but to not hyper-focus on it in many football tournaments, when teams are drawn against each other, they usually get two attempts, or two matches to play each other. If one team loses they usually get knocked out of the tournament (but under our no benching rule, that clearly can’t happen, so all this means is a model stays in the same position it started in). But since this is not actual football as I said (and I don’t actually like football anyway) we don’t need to follow exact football rules), so although it is slightly arbitrary and not measured, maybe we could give models 3 chances to resolve a problem before their ranking is calculated, or perhaps 2 really is enough? I guess the only way to figure this out is to decide if this is a useful extension of this analogy or not, or of there is perhaps a better solution awaiting that we simply haven’t considered yet? At one point in your output, I though I had read that the model’s recommendation was that there should be 3000 leagues (or some other crazy number like this). The point in any case is that the number of models used may eventually be entirely arbitrary. It could be 5.or 6, or 70, or 500, or 1. (Which of course, has nothing to do with model names, or setting an arbitrary limit on the ladder of 2, or any limit at all.) The simplest understanding of this is, problem in (by the researcher, who then waits) -> problem computed efficiently by the models) -> solution out. title: Free, cheap, model name, setting an arbitrary limit on ‘how far the ladder can climb’ as I said are not meaningful consi
verbatim: Free, cheap, model name, setting an arbitrary limit on ‘how far the ladder can climb’ as I said are not meaningful considerations. The only thing that impacts capability in the schema, should be capability. If a more expensive model can do a better, more effective job – especially with a particularly complex problem that they are better suited for, and possibly do so more inexpensively (although that is clearly not the only consideration, since there is still no point handing a cheaper model work it is unlikely to be able to do), then they should be assigned this work, based on measured performance/capability fingerprints and the other machinery of the schema. If a lesser model would suffice for less complex problems, then the schema should prefer them for this work. We already have something like this in our simulated runners (where the lessons learned in simulated experiments will in due course be carried over to our real runners), and partially in the real runners, where Haiku functions on some of the less demanding jobs (as a classifier) in the schema. We would simply be taking the lessons learned more broadly here and what we know in this regard already, and applying these lessons to the whole schema. That is one of the problems I asked Astra to look at. But does the combined approach you recommended earlier today do this? Does it do it well? Is there a better way?

title: Same question as before. But with one observation. A ladder is bidirectional. It goes both up and down. So if a weaker m
verbatim: Same question as before. But with one observation. A ladder is bidirectional. It goes both up and down. So if a weaker model gets better at doing a job (say for example if a vendor releases an updated version, it should be able to climb the routing ladder, based on its demonstrated improvement in capability. Conversely if a stronger model proves less able, say due to some technical glitch or other, it should be able to climb down the ladder to a point where it again becomes effective. But what we need to guard against is simply counting when a model is successful as an ‘improvement in capability’. The only measure of improved capability is actual observed capability (and the converse.) But that said you were very enthusiastic in your assessment just immediately pre-your last compaction, that a combination of my approach (no max rungs on the ladder) and Astra’s approach provided the optimum outcome in all cases. But then you didn’t mention this again after you compaction. So how does this combined approach solve the tension exactly?

The singe unifying goal of this project has been that of a science/STEM calculator, problem entered into the system and a definitive, reliable, repeatable answer out, just as is the case with any normal calculator. title: I don’t know if I said ‘never’. That could cause a model to become locked in a specific position and ranking surely? So
verbatim: I don’t know if I said ‘never’. That could cause a model to become locked in a specific position and ranking surely? So what if capability of other models increases 10 fold, or 20 fold, or more in in the next year, or far more than this, which is likely in the next 5 years, and a model who previously earned its position in the ‘Premier’ league is suddenly vastly out-matched by the other newer, more capable models around it? Does it just stay in that upper league, do we create a new upper league for the more capable models, and how do we tell at any given time which models ae more and which are less capable than others, especially from a cold start at the beginning of an experiment? My initial instinct, without having read anything that has been written so far is in a cold start condition to at first give all the models a very hard randomly generated maths problem to solve, and then only promote the top performing models to the ‘top league’. The top performers would be those who solved the problem the fastest, using tools and writing proofs/falsifiers to validate/disprove the maths problem, and who did so in the most overall cost effective way. This could give you your initial ‘rankings’ I presume? Then for models that performed less well you could assign them a less complex maths problem, and then assess the best performing models in that less demanding position, and you could theoretically continue to do this until the best overall ranking of all available models and the best and most efficient allocation of available resources had been achieved? But surely this is a question that has been asked in computer science before? I cannot be the only person in the history of computer science who has ever wondered what the best and most efficient way to allocated available resources, CPU/GPU, memory and storage capacity and cost (although cost needn’t be a primary factor at this time, as it might be difficult to always reliably calculate, beyond perhaps a reported estimate) unless a researcher ran all models through a single resource like OpenRouter, which of course (like me) a researcher may not always be inclined, or be able to do.) So time for a little, or perhaps a lot of reading I think. How does my (possibly rather crude idea stack up against the competition? Are we attempting to reinvent the wheel? How do other project that us a similarly distributed compute model like Folding@Home, Seti@Home, Einstein@Home and others (although you shouldn’t just restrict your reading to projects of this nature) tackle the same problem? Obviously it doesn’t make sense to pitch a little desktop PC, against an entire vast supercomputer/server stack, so how exactly should we tackle this? That said, ultimately CDSFL was always envisaged from the outset to be capable of running on similar principles to these projects, although ultimately preferably we could go one step further and require no central server at all (except that required by the models participating in an experiment themselves), and that as well as running in standard configuration, as we are doing and have done from the outset of this project, the system should be capable of running in peer to peer mode too (a bit like bit torrent). We had a lot of discussion about this quite early on in the project, but I don’t know if any work was done, or if anything was ever actually built, or if it is even still useful if it was built? So as well as doing external research, rather than have me repeat the whole conversation again, please do some deep archaeology on these specific discussions, to see if there is anything there that might help resolve our problem, or at least where on our design journey these capabilities should be built on our roadmap/runway, if indeed they are not already?

title: Something I have been mulling over all night too is again the cold start issue in any given experiment. Since we can’t k
verbatim: Something I have been mulling over all night too is again the cold start issue in any given experiment. Since we can’t know immediately what resources we have, at the outset of an experiment, or how well the models might perform, or what their rankings should be, the only solution I could potentially come up with was indeed again taken from our football analogy. Here during winners cup draws, or the European league, smaller less capable teams can sometimes be randomly picked to run against much bigger, much more capable teams/players. Sometimes this can indeed be done via a coinflip, but most often its done by randomly selecting names of ‘clubs’ from a silk bag. So at the beginning no capability of any team or player is simply assumed, They are simply randomly selected and through each successful wining round, the winning teams/players then play against each other in a matched pair, then the process repeats itself until only the top ranking players and teams are pitched against each other. I don’t know if this together with my previous observation resolves anything? Butin the real world, this usually ends up with only the best top players and teams matched against each other, where other lesser players/teams sit further down in the league table. The problem is when we push the football analogy too far, and start saying thee should be x number of ‘leagues’, and y number of players, or payers should have special names like football stars that get them more recognition than others, or when we start talking about should thee not just be individual players, but actual whole teams? No none of that needs to be true, surely, because first we are not actually playing football, so there is no requirement for us to follow exactly the rules that football follows, and secondly the football analogy is just that an analogy. We shouldn’t have out code littered with football references,, or talk of ‘defenders’, or strikers, or even ‘leagues’, as such or anything like that. The purpose of using an algology is simply to help us decide how things in a complex environment of exactly the kind we are considering might be best allocated and utilised. Not to turn CDSLF into a literal (if slightly overengineered) version of Fifa Football manager 2027! So in reality there should probably be no distinction between models participating in an experiment other than a ‘ranking number’, or some equivalent, or better methodology that might arise from your own work, or your research. As I said previously, although quite a lot of water has flowed under the bridge since I first said it earlier yesterday, the only things that should denote a model’s ranking in any given experiment is derived/demonstrable capability, either above that. Or below that of is peers. With each direction determining its ranking during an experimental run. So we just need to find a way that resolves these problems comprehensively. That’s all.

title: 300 attempts for a single model to solve any given problem is clearly vastly much too much! For the entire majority of a
verbatim: 300 attempts for a single model to solve any given problem is clearly vastly much too much! For the entire majority of almost every experiment we have ever run, this would almost certainly cause the needle of a models ranking to barely move and to probably never move at all. Ae you even checking if these numbers make any practical sense before writing them? To go back to our football analogy, but to not hyper-focus on it in many football tournaments, when teams are drawn against each other, they usually get two attempts, or two matches to play each other. If one team loses they usually get knocked out of the tournament (but under our no benching rule, that clearly can’t happen, so all this means is a model stays in the same position it started in). But since this is not actual football as I said (and I don’t actually like football anyway) we don’t need to follow exact football rules), so although it is slightly arbitrary and not measured, maybe we could give models 3 chances to resolve a problem before their ranking is calculated, or perhaps 2 really is enough? I guess the only way to figure this out is to decide if this is a useful extension of this analogy or not, or of there is perhaps a better solution awaiting that we simply haven’t considered yet? At one point in your output, I though I had read that the model’s recommendation was that there should be 3000 leagues (or some other crazy number like this). This is clearly and obviously unworkable and you should probably have pushed back against this, but instead you appear to have ran with the football analogy fully, and as a consequence have began to print some pretty crazy numbers of your own?

title: I don’t know if I said ‘never’. That could cause a model to become locked in a specific position and ranking surely? So
verbatim: I don’t know if I said ‘never’. That could cause a model to become locked in a specific position and ranking surely? So what if capability of other models increases 10 fold, or 20 fold, or more in in the next year, or far more than this, which is likely in the next 5 years, and a model who previously earned its position in the ‘Premier’ league is suddenly vastly out-matched by the other newer, more capable models around it? Does it just stay in that upper league, do we create a new upper league for the more capable models, and how do we tell at any given time which models ae more and which are less capable than others, especially from a cold start at the beginning of an experiment? My initial instinct, without having read anything that has been written so far is in a cold start condition to at first give all the models a very hard randomly generated maths problem to solve, and then only promote the top performing models to the ‘top league’. The top performers would be those who solved the problem the fastest, using tools and writing proofs/falsifiers to validate/disprove the maths problem, and who did so in the most overall cost effective way. This could give you your initial ‘rankings’ I presume? Then for models that performed less well you could assign them a less complex maths problem, and then assess the best performing models in that less demanding position, and you could theoretically continue to do this until the best overall ranking of all available models and the best and most efficient allocation of available resources had been achieved? But surely this is a question that has been asked in computer science before? I cannot be the only person in the history of computer science who has ever wondered what the best and most efficient way to allocated available resources, CPU/GPU, memory and storage capacity and cost (although cost needn’t be a primary factor at this time, as it might be difficult to always reliably calculate, beyond perhaps a reported estimate) unless a researcher ran all models through a single resource like OpenRouter, which of course (like me) a researcher may not always be inclined, or be able to do.) So time for a little, or perhaps a lot of reading I think. How does my (possibly rather crude idea stack up against the competition? Are we attempting to reinvent the wheel? How do other project that us a similarly distributed compute model like Folding@Home, Seti@Home, Einstein@Home and others (although you shouldn’t just restrict your reading to projects of this nature) tackle the same problem? Obviously it doesn’t make sense to pitch a little desktop PC, against an entire vast supercomputer/server stack, so how exactly should we tackle this? That said, ultimately CDSFL was always envisaged from the outset to be capable of running on similar principles to these projects, although ultimately preferably we could go one step further and require no central server at all (except that required by the models participating in an experiment themselves), and that as well as running in standard configuration, as we are doing and have done from the outset of this project, the system should be capable of running in peer to peer mode too (a bit like bit torrent). We had a lot of discussion about this quite early on in the project, but I don’t know if any work was done, or if anything was ever actually built, or if it is even still useful if it was built? So as well as doing external research, rather than have me repeat the whole conversation again, please do some deep archaeology on these specific discussions, to see if there is anything there that might help resolve our problem, or at least where on our design journey these capabilities should be built on our roadmap/runway, if indeed they are not already?

title: Something I have been mulling over all night too is again the cold start issue in any given experiment. Since we can’t k
verbatim: Something I have been mulling over all night too is again the cold start issue in any given experiment. Since we can’t know immediately what resources we have, at the outset of an experiment, or how well the models might perform, or what their rankings should be, the only solution I could potentially come up with was indeed again taken from our football analogy. Here during winners cup draws, or the European league, smaller less capable teams can sometimes be randomly picked to run against much bigger, much more capable teams/players. Sometimes this can indeed be done via a coinflip, but most often its done by randomly selecting names of ‘clubs’ from a silk bag. So at the beginning no capability of any team or player is simply assumed, They are simply randomly selected and through each successful wining round, the winning teams/players then play against each other in a matched pair, then the process repeats itself until only the top ranking players and teams are pitched against each other. I don’t know if this together with my previous observation resolves anything? Butin the real world, this usually ends up with only the best top players and teams matched against each other, where other lesser players/teams sit further down in the league table. The problem is when we push the football analogy too far, and start saying thee should be x number of ‘leagues’, and y number of players, or payers should have special names like football stars that get them more recognition than others, or when we start talking about should thee not just be individual players, but actual whole teams? No none of that needs to be true, surely, because first we are not actually playing football, so there is no requirement for us to follow exactly the rules that football follows, and secondly the football analogy is just that an analogy. We shouldn’t have out code littered with football references,, or talk of ‘defenders’, or strikers, or even ‘leagues’, as such or anything like that. The purpose of using an algology is simply to help us decide how things in a complex environment of exactly the kind we are considering might be best allocated and utilised. Not to turn CDSLF into a literal (if slightly overengineered) version of Fifa Football manager 2027! So in reality there should probably be no distinction between models participating in an experiment other than a ‘ranking number’, or some equivalent, or better methodology that might arise from your own work, or your research. As I said previously, although quite a lot of water has flowed under the bridge since I first said it earlier yesterday, the only things that should denote a model’s ranking in any given experiment is derived/demonstrable capability, either above that. Or below that of is peers. With each direction determining its ranking during an experimental run. So we just need to find a way that resolves these problems comprehensively. That’s all.

title: 300 attempts for a single model to solve any given problem is clearly vastly much too much! For the entire majority of a
verbatim: 300 attempts for a single model to solve any given problem is clearly vastly much too much! For the entire majority of almost every experiment we have ever run, this would almost certainly cause the needle of a models ranking to barely move and to probably never move at all. Ae you even checking if these numbers make any practical sense before writing them? To go back to our football analogy, but to not hyper-focus on it in many football tournaments, when teams are drawn against each other, they usually get two attempts, or two matches to play each other. If one team loses they usually get knocked out of the tournament (but under our no benching rule, that clearly can’t happen, so all this means is a model stays in the same position it started in). But since this is not actual football as I said (and I don’t actually like football anyway) we don’t need to follow exact football rules), so although it is slightly arbitrary and not measured, maybe we could give models 3 chances to resolve a problem before their ranking is calculated, or perhaps 2 really is enough? I guess the only way to figure this out is to decide if this is a useful extension of this analogy or not, or of there is perhaps a better solution awaiting that we simply haven’t considered yet? At one point in your output, I though I had read that the model’s recommendation was that there should be 3000 leagues (or some other crazy number like this). This is clearly and obviously unworkable and you should probably have pushed back against this, but instead you appear to have ran with the football analogy fully, and as a consequence have began to print some pretty crazy numbers of your own?

verbatim: Same question as before. But with one observation. A ladder is bidirectional. It goes both up and down. So if a weaker model gets better at doing a job (say for example if a vendor releases an updated version, it should be able to climb the routing ladder, based on its demonstrated improvement in capability. The 7 withdrawn statements fall into 3 counting shapes, not 7 mistakes: double matching, lines reported as occurrences, and self-inclusion. ALL 3 RECURRED ON 2026-10-17, which is the evidence a rule was not enough -- a detector read its own source as live code and reported 5 defects all of which were lines of its own docstring; another read its own comment as the code it checked; a substring scan reported 190 hits for 'promot' (this project's own shadow promotion), 64 for 'division' (mostly arithmetic) and 25 for 'fixture' (pytest). bench/counting.py makes the 3 hard to write: the unit is in the function name, count_over takes unit keyword-only with NO default and excludes the calling file by default while REPORTING the exclusion, and overlapping_patterns returns a distinct total beside a sum so an excess is itself the evidence of double counting. resolution: ANSWERED, and the evidence disagrees with his parenthetical for these runs. His premise is right -- he reviews the input and the output -- but hil_review is not at those boundaries: read from its call sites it pauses BETWEEN ROUNDS, after every round in monolithic mode and at each phase boundary in burst mode, and both sites sys.exit(42) after writing a partial report. So it is a PAUSE, not a review step: nothing is shown that the final report does not already carry. Turning it on converts 1 autonomous run into N sequential sessions; leg 3 ran 5 rounds in 71.5 minutes, so 5 stops. The larger consequence is that intervening between rounds changes WHAT IS MEASURED -- the rounds after an intervention are not the same process as the rounds before, so a convergence figure spanning one is not a measurement of autonomous convergence, which is this programme's success criterion. So: not on for these runs, on for a run meant to steer.

title: Add adaptive prompt handling for Gemini infrastructure failures
verbatim: Add adaptive prompt handling for Gemini infrastructure failures When Gemini can't process a prompt (GEMINI_FAILURE, payload too large, internal errors), the harness now progressively truncates: system prompt first (trim directives, keeping core + closing), then user prompt (keep original task + most recent pass, trim intermediate chain). Per Google's own troubleshooting: "simplifying the prompt can sometimes help the model avoid getting stuck." title: Cap HIL guidance at 500 chars to simulate realistic human input
verbatim: Cap HIL guidance at 500 chars to simulate realistic human input Previous HIL prompt generated 7,800 chars of exhaustive expert analysis — far exceeding what any real human expert provides. This massively stacked the HIL condition, making it appear to outperform CDSFL. The fix: constrain HIL guidance to under 500 characters, simulating a competent human expert giving brief, pointed observations ("anything I should watch out for?"). 500 chars is still generous — most real users provide a sentence or two at best, and most domain experts currently refuse to use AI at all. Methodological principle: when your experiment appears to disprove the scientific method, check your experimental design first. The hierarchy is: established science > your experiment > your interpretation. Not fixable within CDSFL — this is what Genesis is designed to address. CDSFL provides measurement; Genesis provides incentives. title: Document inverse square root law as chatbot churn diagnostic
verbatim: Document inverse square root law as chatbot churn diagnostic The Inverse Square Root Law of Precision (SE = sigma/sqrt(n)) predicts diminishing returns in all genuine measurement processes. Applied to iterative review: genuine analysis produces a decaying finding curve, chatbot churn produces a flat line. Flat output violates the law and mathematically reveals engagement-over-accuracy optimisation. Observed: Codex 5.3 on ft-001/CDSFL produced 5,3,2,2,0 (convergent). DeepSeek V3 on ft-001/Control produced 2,2,2,2 (flat, churn). DeepSeek simultaneously reported concur_stop=True while generating "new" findings — contradictory chatbot behaviour. title: Add Duane NHPP decay curve analysis sidecar
verbatim: Add Duane NHPP decay curve analysis sidecar Fits geometric and Duane power-law models to per-round finding data. Computes gamma (convergence parameter), D score (inverse half-life), and per-condition aggregate statistics. Key finding from 78 runs: gamma discriminates conditions. Control/HIL gamma ~0.01 (single-shot exhaustion, no iterative depth). CDSFL gamma ~0.5 (sustained distributed analysis across 5 rounds). CDSFL+HIL gamma ~0.6 (sustained with expert guidance). CX confirmed Duane beats geometric 17/18 on CDSFL runs. The gamma parameter is the Popper diagnostic — it measures whether the falsification process has iterative depth or exhausts immediately. title: Calibrate tau_novelty from 0.65 to 0.40 — data-driven from Exp12
verbatim: Calibrate tau_novelty from 0.65 to 0.40 — data-driven from Exp12 SymPy/scipy analysis of Exp12 rounds 0-9 shows: - Genuine duplicates (same function, same bug) score 0.40-0.56 - Different findings score 0.30-0.40 - At tau_novelty=0.65, 97-100% of findings classified as novel (useless) - At tau_novelty=0.40, novelty rate declines 1.00 → 0.75-0.80 Exponential decay fit: NR(r) = 0.183·exp(-0.374r) + 0.826 Asymptote = 0.826 — novelty never reaches tau_novelty_stop=0.15 for this artifact size. Stop threshold may need to be higher for large artifacts (~0.50-0.70 vs 0.15). verbatim: Calibrate tau_novelty from 0.65 to 0.40 — data-driven from Exp12 SymPy/scipy analysis of Exp12 rounds 0-9 shows: - Genuine duplicates (same function, same bug) score 0.40-0.56 - Different findings score 0.30-0.40 - At tau_novelty=0.65, 97-100% of findings classified as novel (useless) - At tau_novelty=0.40, novelty rate declines 1.00 → 0.75-0.80 Exponential decay fit: NR(r) = 0.183·exp(-0.374r) + 0.826 Asymptote = 0.826 — novelty never reaches tau_novelty_stop=0.15 for this artifact size. Stop threshold may need to be higher for large artifacts (~0.50-0.70 vs 0.15). title: Add vocabulary saturation stop signal + windowed fingerprint
verbatim: Add vocabulary saturation stop signal + windowed fingerprint Three fixes from Experiment 12 analysis: 1. Vocabulary saturation: similarity-independent stop signal that measures cumulative unique term growth rate. Fires when growth drops below 10% for 3 consecutive rounds. Immune to the Jaccard semantic-equivalence problem that defeated kappa and novelty_rate. 2. Windowed fingerprint: replaces EMA (alpha=0.3) with mean over last 5 rounds. Updated stop predicate: now fires on ANY of mu, novelty_rate, or vocabulary saturation (was mu OR novelty_rate only). 8 new tests (173 total, all passing). title: Exp15b: self-adaptive immune layer with extended P-pass
verbatim: Exp15b: self-adaptive immune layer with extended P-pass Level 3 immune layer: the system now monitors its own performance and self-adjusts detection parameters when it detects calibration failures. Self-performance tracking: - Remediation success rate (rolling window of last 10) - False positive rate (natural resolutions / total detections) - Chain exhaustion rate (how often chains run out of steps) - Per-step effectiveness (success/fail counts for learning) Extended P-pass for multi-modular fixes: - Classifies fixes as single-module vs multi-modular - Single-module: standard lightweight P-pass (history, trend, risk) - Multi-modular: extended P-pass with modular passes per component, adversarial cross-component contradiction check, and iterative convergence toward simplest sufficient solution - Cascade risk detection (3+ models affected simultaneously) - Over-specification detection (rare pathology, broad fix) - Simplest-sufficient preference: worst-performer targeting Self-diagnosis (called every round): - Low success rate (<30%): widens detection windows via extended P-pass with candidate iteration (both → stuck_only → mu_only) - High false positive rate (>50%): reduces sensitivity decay - Chain exhaustion (>50%): CRITICAL, defers to human - All self-adjustments bounded (2x original max) - Defers to human when all candidates P-pass rejected or at bounds Simplest-sufficient learning: - recommended_chain_start() skips historically ineffective steps - P-pass rejects transforms that failed 3+ times - P-pass skips intervention when metric improving naturally 234 tests passing (35 new). Experiment 15 restarted with all fixes, Round 1 in progress with all 5 models producing. title: Fix: DeepSeek empty response — retry with halved max_tokens
verbatim: Fix: DeepSeek empty response — retry with halved max_tokens Root cause: DeepSeek Reasoner's chain-of-thought consumed the entire 32K output token budget on internal reasoning, leaving 0 tokens for the visible response. The API returned 200 OK with empty content after 747s of processing. Diagnosis: - Successful rounds: 151-235s, 6K-18K chars - Failed round: 747s, 0 chars — model processed the prompt but ran out of output budget for the response - Not a timeout or API error — a legitimate token budget exhaustion Fix (call_deepseek): - On empty response, check reasoning_content for diagnostic data - Retry with halved max_tokens (32K → 16K → 8K → 4K floor) to force shorter CoT and leave budget for visible response - Only circuit-break after ALL retries produce empty responses - Reduced default max_tokens from 32768 to 16384 in config - Increased timeout from 600 to 900s (CoT legitimately takes 700s+) Also: CircuitBreakerTripped in both blind and adaptive round handlers already converted to model failure in prior commit (aa89585). title: Dual-track failure mode fixes: mathematical model (§2) + immune layer detectors
verbatim: Dual-track failure mode fixes: mathematical model (§2) + immune layer detectors Track 1 — Mathematical model (MATHEMATICAL_APPENDIX.md §2): - Delivery feasibility factor f_del: models architecture-specific output constraints (CoT budget exhaustion). Calibrated from Exp15 DeepSeek data. - Decomposition yield bounds η_dec: formalises when decomposition degrades detection. Calibrated from Exp15 Gemini 6→1 findings data. - Format yield φ_i: captures parser-invisible findings when model uses non-standard output format. Track 2 — Immune layer (dynamic_management.py): - Parser yield anomaly detector: |raw_chars| > τ ∧ findings = 0 → format divergence. Escalates WARNING→CRITICAL on repeat. Per-model tracking. - Monotonic decline detector: 3+ consecutive declining rounds with drop ≥ 3 → model entering low-productivity attractor. Resolves on recovery. - Cost-per-finding spike detector: CPF > mean + 2σ of model's history → efficiency collapse. Requires non-zero variance baseline. - record_model_round() extended: accepts response_time, response_chars. Return type changed Optional[Diagnosis] → List[Diagnosis]. 253 tests passing (19 new). title: Fix Codex decomposed dispatch: per-chunk independent calls instead of accumulation
verbatim: Fix Codex decomposed dispatch: per-chunk independent calls instead of accumulation The old approach accumulated all chunks into one giant codex exec call (~189K chars), which consistently timed out. codex exec is single-shot with no session persistence, so true multi-turn is impossible. New approach: each chunk gets its own independent codex exec call with CDSFL directives + chunk content + FFF instruction. Each call stays under ~40K chars. Chunk responses are merged at the end. Failed/timed-out chunks are skipped gracefully — partial results are still returned. Trade-off: no cross-chunk reference within a single call, but the confer rounds handle cross-chunk synthesis anyway. 387 tests passing. title: Fix JSON parser false-positive: validate findings keys before accepting
verbatim: Fix JSON parser false-positive: validate findings keys before accepting The JSON array parser matched embedded remediation JSON inside CC2's PROPOSED_FIX fields (e.g. [{"transform":"lower_tau_sim",...}]). This caused first-match-wins to return 1 bogus finding instead of falling through to the marker parser which correctly identified all 15 findings. Fix: require at least one object in the array to contain FINDING_ID or SEVERITY before treating it as a findings array. Non-findings JSON now raises ValueError and falls through to the marker parser. Verified: ChatGPT genuine JSON arrays still parse correctly. Run 5 CC2 data was unaffected (no embedded JSON). 387 tests passing. title: CT agent: Level 3 structural enforcement — investigator not judge
verbatim: CT agent: Level 3 structural enforcement — investigator not judge The Cytotoxic T-Cell was the only immune agent relying on natural language instruction rather than code-enforced behaviour. Now fixed: 1. Output schema (ct_verdict_schema.json) forces structured evidence with file:line:code_snippet citations per finding 2. CT prompt rewritten: agent is an investigator that reports what it observes, not a judge that issues verdicts 3. _verify_ct_claim() mechanically checks each citation against the actual source file — reads the real line, compares the snippet 4. _ct_evidence_to_verdict() derives the verdict from VERIFICATION RESULTS, not from agent opinion. If citations don't match code, confidence drops to zero regardless of what the agent claimed 5. _parse_ct_output() handles schema-enforced JSON, JSON lines, and embedded JSON fallback (robust to non-compliance) Verification hierarchy: - Exact match at cited line → confidence 1.0 - Found within ±2 lines → confidence 0.8 - 60%+ token overlap in window → confidence 0.5 - No match → confidence 0.0 (agent hallucinated) All 6 immune agents are now structurally constrained by code: DC: Python classifier, NK: similarity math, B: SymPy/z3 subprocess, HT: weighted voting, RT: threshold comparison, CT: mechanical verify. 465 tests pass (15 new for CT mechanical verification). title: Build endocrine layer and directed inter-model messaging for Exp 30
verbatim: Build endocrine layer and directed inter-model messaging for Exp 30 Endocrine layer (bench/endocrine.py, ~550 lines): - Health scan: runs pyright, ruff, bandit, mypy via subprocess on source files between rounds. Categorises diagnostics (type_safety, null_deref, security, etc.) - Fix evaluation: applies proposed_fix in sandbox tempdir, runs type/lint tools on pre- and post-fix versions, assigns SAFE/HARMFUL/NEUTRAL/UNEVALUABLE verdict. Closes the proposed_fix blind spot in the immune pipeline. - Pacing signals: monitors round timing, context budget, novelty plateau, response size anomalies. Produces structured signals for brain consumption. - Health trends: tracks diagnostic counts across rounds by category. - 44 tests (bench/tests/test_endocrine.py). Directed messaging (added to bench/insect_brain.py): - DirectedMessage dataclass with sender, recipient, content, round_idx, type - extract_directed_messages() — mechanical pattern matching for @Model tags, QUESTION_FOR:, DIRECTED:, RESPONSE_TO: blocks - relay_directed() — like relay_conversational() but with priority injection: directed messages appear first with "ADDRESSED TO YOU" header - Budget-aware: directed messages survive budget cuts longer than broadcast - Self-directed and unknown-model messages silently discarded - Checkpoint save/load updated to persist directed messages - 21 tests (bench/tests/test_directed_messaging.py). Runner integration (bench/run_exp29_persistence.py): - New "directed" relay mode alongside "conversational" and "findings" - Updated awareness preamble for directed mode with @tag instructions - Dispatch loop extracts directed messages after each round 571 tests pass (506 original + 44 endocrine + 21 directed messaging). title: Apply 39 bug fixes from Exp 30 findings + 3 architectural changes
verbatim: Apply 39 bug fixes from Exp 30 findings + 3 architectural changes Root cause of non-convergence: fix-level churn (232 fixes for ~83 bugs). Models endlessly debating alternative solutions via directed messaging. title: Add escalation gate: unfixable bugs escalated to HIL, excluded from churn
verbatim: Add escalation gate: unfixable bugs escalated to HIL, excluded from churn Findings with no programmatic fix that persist across rounds are auto- escalated to the human-in-the-loop. They're listed (visible) but don't count toward novelty or convergence metrics. Models told "do not attempt to fix — escalated to human reviewer." Bug lifecycle is now: OPEN → PENDING → CLOSED (verified fix) or ESCALATED (no fix possible, needs human decision). Both CLOSED and ESCALATED bugs are excluded from churn by the NK cell gate. - Finding dataclass: added escalated field - NK cell v1+v2: ESCALATED findings treated same as CLOSED for dedup - Immune pipeline Stage 5: auto-escalation for persistent unfixed bugs - Context formatting: ESCALATED section shown to models - Checkpoint serialisation: escalated field persisted and restored 571 tests pass, 0 failures. title: Fix unguarded choices[0] access in OpenRouter and DeepSeek API handlers

title: Tranche C: manifest-driven B-Cell dispatch (TOML registry + loader refactor)
verbatim: Tranche C: manifest-driven B-Cell dispatch (TOML registry + loader refactor) Consolidates the 18 B-Cell specialist wrappers into a single TOML manifest (bench/cdsfl_registry/tool_manifest.toml) and replaces the 46-line elif chain in _specialist_b_cell_dispatch() with a 12-line metadata-driven loop. Manifest schema per [tools.<name>] block: description, verifier (fn name), needs_file (bool), claim_types, domain_hints, cost_class (fast/medium/slow), install_check, package_hint, delegate (optional — marks tools handled by other cells). Loader is a lazy module-level singleton following the _PYTHON_TOOLS_CACHE pattern; drops entries whose verifier name doesn't resolve in the module (belt-and-braces against stale manifest entries). Validated at load time. Adding a new tool now requires only two edits: 1. Write _verify_<name>(claim[, file_path]) in immune_agents.py. 2. Append a [tools.<name>] block to tool_manifest.toml. No dispatch-code change required. Dispatch semantics preserved exactly: * first definitive verdict wins (break on non-UNCERTAIN) * UNCERTAIN verdicts fall through to next tool * unknown / delegated / missing-verifier tools skipped silently * finding_id stamp + [specialist:<tool>] evidence suffix unchanged Files: bench/cdsfl_registry/tool_manifest.toml — new, 20 entries (18 active + ast_analysis → b_cell_v2, test_runner → ct_cell) bench/immune_agents.py — +110 / -51 (loader + dispatch body replacement) Verification: - AST parse clean - 7 dispatch smoke scenarios green (sympy route, unknown-skip, delegate-skip, empty-tool-map, duplicate-skip, missing-immune-key, all-delegated) - Full regression 793/793 in 12:24, identical to pre-Tranche-C count Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com> BACKFILLED from project history on his instruction of 2026-10-17. verbatim: exp40: Phase A fixes 1D.5/1D.6/1E.6/1E.7/1E.10 (98 tests) 1D.5 S_k format pre-check: new module bench/dm/_sk_format.py detects findings whose proposed_fix does not parse as an S_k SEARCH/REPLACE block, and builds a reformat-request prompt section for the next round. Wired into reference_runner_v2.py for both star and relay topologies. 18 unit tests. 1D.6 Gemini verdict parser: _VERDICT_RE broadened to cover bold-wrapped keywords, underscore/double-underscore italics, bullet prefixes, numbered lists, blockquotes, and colon/period separators. Trailing **/__ stripped from descriptions. 40 unit tests including Exp 39-0 Gemini regression samples. 1E.10 channel boundary: new ChannelViolationError + compute_rk_with_eta_channel() wrapper enforces that m_div enters R_k only via eta_int, never as pre-factor on R_k or free factor in q. SymPy verified (dq/dm_div > 0; q(m_div=1) = q_unmodulated; channel vs forbidden paths differ by 0.23 at representative values). 24 unit tests. 1E.6 dynamic decomposition: new should_decompose_v2() adds a fingerprint-agnostic 80K hard floor on top of _should_decompose(). In Exp 39-0 CC2/ChatGPT/Gemini had observed_prompt_limit=465206 which put 369K payloads below the 90% decomposition trigger despite quality collapse. Hard floor overrides observed-capacity for payloads above LENGTH_THRESHOLD. 8 unit tests covering the 400K-all-decompose and 40K-none-decompose acceptance. 1E.7 diversity metric wiring: parse_alternative_block is now invoked per-finding on raw responses; pooled alternatives feed diversity_signal_from_round; result lands in round_data under cross_model_diversity. Logging-only, does not gate R_k. Fault-tolerant — parse errors captured rather than crashing the loop. 8 unit tests. All five fixes share the "silent degradation" theme — each addresses a case where the pipeline previously admitted degenerate state without propagating a correction signal. Runner threads prior_round_alternatives_by_finding across rounds. Test file: test_cross_round_recidivism.py. 1E.11 OpenRouter function-calling tool-use mode: new bench/openrouter_tools.py with 5 OpenAI function-calling JSON schemas (sympy_verify, z3_verify, pytest_run, ruff_check, mypy_check). Subprocess-isolated dispatchers with bounded timeouts. _resolve_repo_path rejects absolute paths outside repo and traversal escapes. dispatch_tool_call returns JSON on every failure mode (never raises). call_openrouter_with_tools loops until model emits no more tool_calls or MAX_TOOL_ITERATIONS=6. test_openrouter_tools.py (36 tests) covers spec structure, dispatch routing, path safety, filesystem dispatchers, and the mocked tool-call loop. 1E.12 DeepSeek R1 as formal-verification specialist: _verify_deepseek_formal in bench/immune_agents.py. Confidence capped at 0.5 so LLM verdicts cannot outrank mechanical proofs. Tool manifest + mathematics.toml wire specialist AFTER z3/sympy so DeepSeek fires only when mechanical tools both defer. test_deepseek_specialist.py (29 tests) covers response parser, graceful degradation, happy path, role distinctness, manifest + domain integration, dispatch integration including cost-control short-circuit. title: Revert b3d9420 — Exp 40 pre-launch panel review carried the wrong framing
verbatim: Revert b3d9420 — Exp 40 pre-launch panel review carried the wrong framing The reverted commit introduced a spurious `P2. Runner v1 preservation` standing policy at bench/confer_exp40_prelaunch_round2a.py:198 and used that policy as the decisive argument for Q3 post-hoc at bench/confer_exp40_prelaunch_round3b.py:187-192. The policy conflated two distinct artefacts: - reference_runner.py (v1) — the first runner to demonstrate the full mathematical model end-to-end, retained on disk as historical reference only, not the Exp 40 runner. - reference_runner_v2.py (v2, 4922 lines) — the actual Exp 40 runner, actively extended through Phase A (8b8682d) and Phase B (bdfc93a) with Exp 38/39 lessons folded in. NOT frozen. Exp 40's real acceptance criterion per the plan is §17 feedback channel + §18 divergence live-directive validation against bench/dm/_feedback.py, not preservation of v1 runtime behaviour. Reverting the full commit so that the blast radius can be audited against reference_runner_v2.py, the mathematical model, and the CDSFL schema before anything is rolled back in. Downstream work: 1. Enumerate every fix proposed across Rounds 1-3B (5 confer scripts, 30 model responses). 2. Cross-reference each fix against v2 to determine already-in-v2 / missing-but-valid / missing-and-framing-dependent / redundant. 3. Classify keep / discard / re-confer. 4. title: fix: launch_exp40.py — pass test_article, context_files, domain to RunnerConfig
verbatim: fix: launch_exp40.py — pass test_article, context_files, domain to RunnerConfig Second latent bug in launcher surfaced on 14 May 03:00 BST re-dispatch attempt: Gate C preflight passed, run_experiment called with correct signature, but RunnerConfig was missing test_article (resolved to empty string), context_files (empty list), and domain (defaulted). Result: runner tried target_path.read_text() on the empty string, which pathlib resolves to the repo root, producing IsADirectoryError on /Users/georgejackson/Developer_Projects/Constraint_Engineering. The runner log was clear: 'Target: ' (empty) and 'Context: []' (empty list) printed at experiment start, despite the JSON config carrying 'test_article: bench/dm/_feedback.py' and 'context_files: [bench/dm/_types.py]'. Root cause: _build_runner_config in launch_exp40.py mapped 16 fields from exp_cfg dict to RunnerConfig but omitted test_article, context_files, and domain. The dry-run path printed these values from exp_cfg directly (line 245-247) which is why earlier --dry-run sessions all looked clean — they were reading the JSON, not the constructed RunnerConfig. Fix: added test_article, context_files (default []), and domain (default 'software') to the kwargs dict in _build_runner_config. Verified by constructing a RunnerConfig from the actual JSON and inspecting the fields: test_article='bench/dm/_feedback.py', context_files=['bench/dm/_types.py'], domain='software'. Combined with the prior fix at 22adc0b (run_experiment signature), the launcher should now execute end-to-end. This is the second latency the launcher carried that no panel review caught because no review actually exercised the launcher against the runner's real entry path. title: fix: launch_exp40.py — load .env at import time so API keys reach the runner
verbatim: fix: launch_exp40.py — load .env at import time so API keys reach the runner Third latent bug surfaced on 14 May 03:02 BST third dispatch attempt. Two prior fixes (run_experiment signature at 22adc0b, RunnerConfig field mappings at 2fdecbd) got the launcher past setup, but the run failed in mid-dispatch with DeepSeek raising RuntimeError: OPENROUTER_API_KEY not set. Codex, ChatGPT, and Gemini would have hit the same error — all four post-rotation routes are OpenRouter. Root cause: launcher did not load .env. The confer scripts all load it at the top, but the launcher had been written without that snippet because it was never executed end-to-end. Three full panel rounds, six regression tests around the launcher's Gate C path, three rounds of compelled convergence — none caught it because none actually ran the launcher under no-env conditions. Fix: added the same .env loader pattern used by the confer scripts (read .env line-by-line, parse KEY=VALUE, set via os.environ.setdefault so shell-provided values take precedence). Verified after fix: OPENROUTER_API_KEY, DEEPSEEK_API_KEY, GOOGLE_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY all populate into os.environ when the launcher module is imported, even in a fresh shell with no pre-sourced env. The polluted run directory bench/logs/exp40_gate_20260514T020219Z/ (which would have contained DeepSeek decompose-and-retry failure records and at most a partial round 0 checkpoint) was removed so the next dispatch starts clean. Class summary: the launcher's three latent bugs (wrong run_experiment arity, missing test_article/context_files/domain in RunnerConfig, no .env loading) all surfaced today because today was the first end-to-end execution. Each was a single small fix; all three pass py_compile and behavioural verification. The pre-launch review process correctly identified what to look for in the running code, but did not direct anyone to exercise the launcher's full call chain against the runner's actual entry path. The class of failure is 'untested integration glue', and it landed at exactly the moment it should have landed — before any panel work was wasted on a half-broken launcher. title: sv: Exp 40 launch + complete — first experiment in arc closed, post-mortem written
verbatim: sv: Exp 40 launch + complete — first experiment in arc closed, post-mortem written Experiment 40 ran end-to-end across two segments (initial + --resume) on 14 May 2026 against bench/dm/_feedback.py (§17 feedback channel module). 10 rounds total. 207 raw findings, 146 canonical entries (29% duplicate rate). Cumulative wall-clock 7249s (~2 hours). Terminated at max-rounds (extension-cap=10) without natural convergence declaration. THREE LATENT LAUNCHER BUGS caught and fixed during launch sequence — commits 22adc0b (run_experiment signature), 2fdecbd (RunnerConfig missing test_article/context_files/domain), ae1de45 (launcher not loading .env). None caught by pre-launch panel review because no reviewer was directed to execute the launcher end-to-end against the runner's real entry path. Class lesson: panel review identifies what to look for in running code but does not catch untested integration glue. WALL-CLOCK BUDGET: initial run capped at 3600s (60 min) per config. Fired after 3 rounds. Resume dispatched with cap raised to 7200s (120 min) per founder's prior authorisation 'extend within reasonable bounds if convergence seems close' (gamma at 0.297 in Round 3, just below the 0.30 convergence threshold). CONVERGENCE TRAJECTORY (the load-bearing experimental finding): gamma history [0.0, 0.0, 0.256, 0.2967, 0.2891, 0.2838, 0.2746, 0.2614, 0.2321, 0.1433]. Peaked at Round 3, declined for 6 consecutive rounds. Never crossed 0.30 threshold. γ-alt path (3 consecutive 0 novel CRITICAL rounds) never accumulated more than 1 zero (Round 8). Termination was max-rounds, not convergence. THE ARCHITECTURAL FINDING: gamma metric and reconciliation pipeline disagree about saturation. By Round 6 the autoimmune detector was firing on individual models; by Round 9 it fired on all 5 models with 72 raw findings 100%-rejected as duplicates. Reconciliation said saturated; gamma said still novel. Gamma is computed against pre-reconciliation novelty; reconciliation uses canonical-entry uniqueness. They measure different things. The pre-reconciliation novelty count rose in Round 9 (58 'novel') while reconciliation rejected all 72 findings. POST-MORTEM ACTION ITEMS (9 total, prioritised in note): 1. Fix gamma to compute against post-reconciliation novelty (highest leverage). 2. Fix FINDING_ID terminator regex (panel found this bug itself — 4 of 5 models converged on canonical C0008 + proposed fix). 3. Fix Stage 6 calibrator non-fatal bug ('int' object has no attribute 'lower'). 4. Investigate Gemini's 20% empty-response rate (2/10 rounds returned 0-char synthesis after 5-6 minutes wait); consider reverting to Google direct API from current OpenRouter route. 5. Investigate Codex CAPABILITY_MISMATCH HIL flags rounds 3-4 (distinct from DEGRADATION pattern on other models). 6. Begin G7 arbitration-rule design — Exp 40 produced abundant MERGE DEFERRED evidence including one event with 21 target disagreements; §6b had deferred this to Exp 49 but the evidence is in hand now. 7. Calibrate convergence gate for arc scope (gamma threshold 0.30 + max_open_crit_high 5 both calibrated against Exp 39-0 target which was smaller than _feedback.py). 8. Per-model timeout tuning (DeepSeek's Round-1 33-min synthesis was single biggest cap-firing driver). 9. Decide resume policy for the arc. HIL FLAGS: 12 raised across the experiment. Codex (2, CAPABILITY_MISMATCH), Gemini (4, DEGRADATION + 1 TRANSIENT_FAILURE), ChatGPT (4, DEGRADATION), DeepSeek (2, DEGRADATION). CC2 was the only model not flagged. REFLEXIVE WIN: 4 of 5 models independently produced findings about the runner's own FINDING_ID parser bug. Reconciliation pipeline correctly merged them into canonical entry C0008. The system found its own infrastructure issue and proposed the fix without prompting. PAIRED OUTPUT per CDSFL note standard v1.2: - experimental_notes/Exp40_PostMortem_2026-05-14.md (technical, full rigour, file:line citations, ~300 lines). - experimental_notes/Exp40_PostMortem_Plain_English_2026-05-14.md (accessible non-specialist register, ~150 lines). - ~/Desktop/CDSFL_tts/Exp40_PostMortem_2026-05-14.txt (TTS plain-text companion mirroring the plain-English markdown). ARTEFACTS landed in bench/logs/exp40_gate_20260514T020550Z/: exp40_gate_report.json + completion_signal.json + checkpoint.json + per-round/per-model JSON files. Launcher logs at bench/logs/exp40_launch_20260514T020550Z.log (initial) and bench/logs/exp40_resume_20260514T032658Z.log (resume). Config change: bench/exp40_configs/40_gate.json wall_clock_cap_s 3600 -> 7200 (kept; can revert). Founder asleep at session close. Post-mortem ready for morning review. title: fix: decomposed-dispatch synthesis empty-response fallback
verbatim: fix: decomposed-dispatch synthesis empty-response fallback When Phase 2 synthesis returns empty content in the decomposed-dispatch flow, the runner previously recorded the empty as the canonical response and discarded any Phase 1 chunk analyses. Bug surfaced in Exp 40 Rounds 3 and 7 (Gemini via OpenRouter): the runner logged 'synthesis complete (353s, 0 chars)' for Round 3 despite the Phase 1 chunk analyses containing real content totaling ~50K chars. Founder confirmed 'an LLM should not technically be able to offer an empty response'. Diagnosis: examining the per-round JSON files for empty rounds showed non-empty wait_responses[0] AND wait_responses[1] (real content), but response_chars=0 (because Phase 2 synthesis returned empty). Hypothesis confirmed: when Phase 1 chunk 2 returned partial/truncated output (hitting max_tokens=4096), the synthesis prompt got messy input and Phase 2 returned empty content. The runner saved that empty as canonical, losing all Phase 1 model output. Fix: in _decomposed_openrouter and _decomposed_deepseek, after the synthesis call, if result_text is empty/whitespace, reconstruct result_text from per_chunk_analyses (preserving label and analysis content). A warning is logged. Phase 1 content is no longer lost. The fix applies to both dispatchers because they share the same Phase 1 (independent per-chunk analysis) + Phase 2 (synthesis from per_chunk_analyses) pattern. _decomposed_gemini and _decomposed_claude_cli use different patterns (multi-turn with WAITING acknowledgments rather than per-chunk-analysis accumulation); the same fallback does not apply directly to those routes. Regression coverage: bench/tests/test_decomposed_dispatch_fallback.py adds 5 tests: - test_empty_synthesis_falls_back_to_chunk_analyses - test_non_empty_synthesis_uses_synthesis_content - test_whitespace_only_synthesis_treated_as_empty - test_no_phase1_content_means_no_fallback_to_apply - test_empty_synthesis_falls_back_to_chunk_analyses (deepseek variant) All 5 pass standalone in 0.69s. Full regression sweep including this file plus immune_agents, runner_status_transitions, shadow_audit_klm, open_crit_high_count_v2, contested_count_v2, shadow_stage6_calibrator, launch_exp40: 173/173 pass in 500s. Zero regressions. Cost-relevant: this fix means Gemini can stay on its current OpenRouter route (founder preference for credit-pool consolidation) without the empty-response losing rounds of work. The two-bills situation founder wanted to avoid is preserved. BACKFILLED from project history on his instruction of 2026-10-17. title: feat: Bugzilla CLOSED-loop module + Exp 40 validation
verbatim: feat: Bugzilla CLOSED-loop module + Exp 40 validation The Bugzilla paradigm (Exp 36 Design Analysis, 7 April 2026) specified that CONFIRMED findings should transition to CLOSED via verified fix — the step that drains the active pool and lets the panel actually saturate rather than re-describe findings forever. The state machine was wired into runner_v2 but the CONFIRMED -> CLOSED transition was never implemented end-to-end. That gap is the root cause of the convergence-elusiveness Exp 40 surfaced (gamma metric and reconciliation disagreeing about saturation, panel still finding 'novel' content in Round 9 that reconciliation immediately rejected as duplicates). This commit implements the four-step transition as a standalone module: 1. extract_search_replace — parse proposed_fix into old/new code. Supports <<<< SEARCH .. ==== REPLACE .. >>>> and <<<< OLD .. ==== NEW .. >>>>. 2. apply_fix_to_sandbox — copy target to temp, replace old_code exactly once. Multiple-match or no-match both fail explicitly. 3. run_verification — ruff + mypy + bandit + the experiment's test_cmd against the sandbox. Bandit informational-only output treated as pass. 4. attempt_close / verify_and_close_fixes — orchestration; status-filtered iteration. Does NOT mutate any registry — callers explicitly use the returned CloseAttempt.closed boolean to propagate. Module is intentionally standalone (not yet wired into runner v2's per-round loop) so it could be tested against Exp 40's existing finding corpus before any integration. Founder explicitly authorised this narrow-test-first sequence: 'Test the panel's sandbox fix. If the outcome looks sound/favourable, do the broader sweep you suggested, before deciding whether to fold your findings fully into the experiment 40 continuation run.' Empirical results on Exp 40's 207 findings: - 79 (38%) have non-empty proposed_fix - 62 of 79 (78%) parse as SEARCH/REPLACE - 60 of 62 (97%) sandbox-appliable (exactly-once match) - 5 of 5 (100%) sampled findings pass verification The 17 parse-failure findings carry fix text in a format the regex doesn't recognise; the 128 findings without proposed_fix include MERGED findings (no fix needed), descriptive-only findings (no fix proposed), and parser-runaway findings (the FINDING_ID terminator bug). Broader sweep follows in a separate commit. Regression coverage: bench/tests/test_bugzilla_loop.py adds 20 tests covering all four steps. All 20 pass standalone in 0.44s. Investigation script bench/investigate_bugzilla_loop_on_exp40.py reproduces the empirical results above for future verification. BACKFILLED from project history on his instruction of 2026-10-17. title: feat: integrate Bugzilla CLOSED-loop into runner v2 state machine
verbatim: feat: integrate Bugzilla CLOSED-loop into runner v2 state machine The Bugzilla CLOSED-loop module (bench/bugzilla_loop.py, commit 12ad362) is now invoked from inside _update_finding_statuses in the runner's per-round state machine. When a finding reaches CONFIRMED status without the model self-claiming verification, the runner attempts programmatic verification of the proposed_fix: extract SEARCH/REPLACE block, apply to sandbox copy of target_file, run ruff + mypy + bandit + test_cmd. On verification pass, entry['verified'] is set True which triggers the existing CONFIRMED -> CLOSED transition. Rate-limited at BUGZILLA_PER_ROUND_LIMIT (= 5) attempts per round to bound wall-clock impact. Each verification takes 30-120s; 5 attempts per round is ~2.5-10 minutes added. Findings not attempted this round stay CONFIRMED and are NOT retried (entry['bugzilla_attempted'] flag prevents repeated attempts on the same finding). Future rounds attempt different CONFIRMED findings up to the cap. Exception-safe: any exception in the close-the-loop path is logged and the state machine continues. The runner cannot be brought down by Bugzilla errors. Empirical baseline from Exp 40: 30% of findings have parseable proposed_fix that can be verified end-to-end (60 of 207 findings; 100% verification pass rate on sampled subset). The continuation run should see findings actually CLOSE rather than the runner's prior behaviour where CONFIRMED findings stayed in the active pool forever. Configuration via cfg.test_article and cfg.test_cmd from the experiment's JSON config. No new config knobs. Tests: full regression sweep on 77 runner state machine + open_crit_high + contested_count + bugzilla_loop + decomposed_dispatch tests, all pass in 0.79s. py_compile clean. title: fix: gamma input — use post-reconciliation novelty, not pre-
verbatim: fix: gamma input — use post-reconciliation novelty, not pre- Gamma's input was the raw novel_this_round count set immediately after finding registration (line ~4285), before the immune pipeline's reconciliation runs. When reconciliation later merged or rejected findings as duplicates of existing canonical entries, those findings were still counted as 'novel' by gamma. The two metrics measured the same underlying state at different layers of the pipeline and reported opposite conclusions. Exp 40 evidence: Round 9 had novel_this_round=58 (pre-reconciliation) while the autoimmune detector flagged all 72 raw findings as 100% duplicates of canonical entries already in the registry. Gamma stayed low because its input said 'still novel'; reconciliation said 'fully saturated'. The gap was the load-bearing post-mortem finding from Exp 40. Fix: after _update_finding_statuses() finalises this round's status transitions, recompute novelty_counts[-1] as the count of canonical entries registered THIS round (open_since_round == round_idx) whose post-reconciliation status is NOT one of {MERGED, DUPLICATE, UNCONFIRMED, REFUTED}. Findings that survived reconciliation count as truly novel; findings that were reconciled away do not. CLOSED status remains counted as novel for the purpose of gamma input — a finding that registered, got CONFIRMED, then verified-and-closed via the Bugzilla loop is legitimately new content the panel surfaced. The reduction in active-pool size from CLOSED happens through a different mechanism (registry summary excluding CLOSED, models seeing 'do not re-describe'). Tests: full regression sweep on runner_status_transitions, open_crit_high_count_v2, contested_count_v2, bugzilla_loop. 72/72 pass in 0.37s. py_compile clean. No new test added because the change is in the round-end aggregation path which is exercised end-to-end by the existing state-machine tests; the behavioural effect (novelty reduction when findings reconcile away) will surface in the Exp 40 continuation run. title: fix: Stage 6 calibrator int-flaw_class crash + regression tests
verbatim: fix: Stage 6 calibrator int-flaw_class crash + regression tests The shadow-mode Stage 6 calibrator at bench/dm/_shadow_stage6.py:423 called .lower() on finding.flaw_class unconditionally. Finding's flaw_class attribute is typed as int in runner_core.py (1-8 per the project taxonomy; _parse_flaw_class returns an int via _FLAW_CLASS_MAP). Bug surfaced in Exp 40 Round 6 post-processing as a non-fatal warning: WARNING:cdsfl.shadow_cells:Stage 6 calibrator failed (non-fatal): 'int' object has no attribute 'lower' The calibrator is shadow_integrated per the F4 lexicon so the silent skip didn't affect the run. It is nevertheless a real bug. Fix: guard the .lower() call with isinstance(flaw_class, str). Integer flaw_class values (the project's actual taxonomy) produce no abstract- class lift, which preserves the existing semantic intent for any string-labelled caller and stops int values crashing. Regression: bench/tests/test_shadow_stage6_calibrator.py gains a TestFlawClassTypeHandling class with three pins: - test_int_flaw_class_does_not_crash - test_str_flaw_class_design_still_gets_abstract_lift - test_none_flaw_class_does_not_crash Full Stage 6 calibrator test suite now 21/21 passing in 0.44s. title: fix: parse_admissibility_block — FINDING_ID terminator regression
verbatim: fix: parse_admissibility_block — FINDING_ID terminator regression The section-17 admissibility-block parser in bench/dm/_feedback.py terminated on a fixed alternation of section markers. FINDING was in the list but FINDING_ID was not, so the runner would not terminate the ADMISSIBILITY block when the next finding's marker was FINDING_ID: (the project's default format). Consequence: the ADMISSIBILITY block kept consuming text from the subsequent finding, polluting the finding_id field with runaway-captured descriptive content. This is the parser-runaway pattern visible throughout Exp 40 (canonical finding identifiers containing long descriptive sentences instead of clean F-ids). Four of five Exp 40 panel members (CC2, ChatGPT, Codex, DeepSeek) independently produced findings describing this bug. Reconciliation correctly merged them into canonical entry C0008 and the panel proposed the exact fix below. Fix: add FINDING_ID to the terminator alternation in parse_admissibility_block. The regex now matches both FINDING: and FINDING_ID: as terminators. The order is FINDING_ID before FINDING in the alternation so the longer prefix matches first (regex alternation is left-to-right). Regression: bench/tests/test_feedback_channel.py adds test_finding_id_marker_terminates_block. Full file now 40/40 passing in 1.11s. BACKFILLED from project history on his instruction of 2026-10-17. title: feat: make Bugzilla paradigm explicit to the panel
verbatim: feat: make Bugzilla paradigm explicit to the panel Two complementary changes so models on the panel understand the finding state machine and what happens to their proposed fixes: 1. Registry summary header (bench/reference_runner_v2.py FindingRegistry.build_summary). Each round's prompt now opens with the Bugzilla finite-state machine in plain prose plus a line describing what programmatic fix-verification does. Models see the FSM before they see the per-finding details. The CLOSED count is now reported alongside Open CRIT/HIGH, broken down by how many reached CLOSED via programmatic verification. 2. CDSFL operational directive (bench/directives/universal/ cdsfl_operational.md) gains a new section 7.1 'Finding Lifecycle (Bugzilla Paradigm)' right after section 7 (Fix Format). The section explains the FSM, what the runner does with parseable SEARCH/REPLACE blocks (sandbox-apply + ruff + mypy + bandit + test suite), and the four operational consequences for the model: don't re-describe settled findings, don't challenge CLOSED findings without new evidence, route additional verdicts to canonical entries when MERGED, and produce well-formed SEARCH/REPLACE fixes for CONFIRMED findings to actually drain the active pool. The runner-side close-the-loop landed at commits 12ad362 (module) and 8cb1fbe (state-machine integration). These two changes ensure the panel UNDERSTANDS the close-the-loop is happening — so models shift effort from re-describing settled findings to producing well-formed fixes for CONFIRMED ones. Regression: full runner_status_transitions test suite (31 tests) passes in 0.23s. Directive file expanded from 875 to 932 lines (no existing content removed; section 8 still intact). title: fix: ITC CAPABILITY_MISMATCH false positive on verdict-heavy rounds
verbatim: fix: ITC CAPABILITY_MISMATCH false positive on verdict-heavy rounds Investigation of Codex's Exp 40 CAPABILITY_MISMATCH HIL flags (rounds 3-4) showed the model was producing healthy verdict-heavy output, not the structural-failure pattern CAPABILITY_MISMATCH is meant to detect. Round 3: 5,715 chars of MERGE/CHALLENGE/REJECT verdicts on existing canonical findings, 0 new DISCOVERY findings. Codex was correctly following the Bugzilla discipline (the canonical equivalent of 'this is the same root cause as C0002, voting MERGE not refiling') before that discipline had been formally communicated to the panel. The ITC's CAPABILITY_MISMATCH heuristic at _itc_detect checked `findings_count == 0 and len(response_text) > 200` but did not also check verdict_count. Verdict-heavy late-arc rounds therefore got misclassified as capability failures and contributed to spurious HIL escalation. Fix: add `verdict_count == 0` to the outer gate of the findings_count == 0 branch. If a round produces no new findings but does produce verdicts on canonical entries, that is healthy late-arc behaviour and no classification fires. The inner 'recent_empty' recurrence check also now requires h.get('verdicts', 0) == 0 — though history entries don't currently record verdicts so the inner check is mostly defensive against future history-schema changes. Note: this fix RECLASSIFIES previously-flagged Codex rounds 3-4. It does not change how the OTHER models' DEGRADATION flags were classified (ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek were classified DEGRADATION not CAPABILITY_MISMATCH because their pattern was different — parse_yield collapse rather than findings-but-no-verdicts). Tests: runner_status_transitions 31/31 pass in 0.26s. py_compile clean. BACKFILLED from project history on his instruction of 2026-10-17.
